REP: Rosa, thanks for squeezing me in. I know Tuesdays are your delivery day, so I'll keep it tight. Can I start with a couple of questions about your front store?
CUSTOMER: Go ahead. The delivery's late anyway.
REP: How are home blood pressure monitors selling for you right now?
CUSTOMER: Slowly. We carry the big national brand at fifty-nine ninety-nine and we sell maybe three a month between both stores. People look at the box, look at the price, and put it back. The second store sells even fewer, because it has a smaller front end.
REP: When someone puts it back, what do you think is going on for them?
CUSTOMER: Mostly price. A lot of our customers are retirees on fixed incomes. Their doctor tells them to check their pressure at home, they come here, and sixty dollars feels like a lot for something they're not sure they'll use. Some of them are choosing between that and their copays that month. I don't blame them.
REP: And what happens with those customers after they walk away from the shelf?
CUSTOMER: Some of them buy online. Some of them just don't check at all, and then I see them at the counter with a new blood pressure prescription and no idea what their numbers look like at home. It's frustrating, honestly. We do a lot of hypertension counseling here. Half my questions at the counter are about blood pressure.
REP: It sounds like counseling is a big part of how you see your role. How do you use home readings in those conversations today?
CUSTOMER: When people bring a log, it's great. I can see if the new medication is working and flag it for the doctor. But maybe one in five has a log. The rest just say they feel fine. Which, with blood pressure, tells me nothing. Feeling fine is the whole problem.
REP: That's really helpful. The BP-200 might fit that gap. It's an upper-arm monitor that stores readings for two people, it retails at forty-four ninety-nine, and your cost is twenty-two dollars, so you make more per unit than on the national brand while charging fifteen dollars less.
CUSTOMER: I like the price point. My problem is space. My front counter is already a mess and I don't have an empty shelf anywhere.
REP: I hear you. Front-store space is the scarcest thing you've got. Which items on that blood pressure shelf actually move?
CUSTOMER: The national brand barely moves, like I said. The cuff refills and the pill organizers move, because I recommend them at the counter. The wrist monitors have been sitting there since spring. I keep meaning to mark them down.
REP: Then one option is to swap out the wrist monitors instead of finding new space. The countertop display holds four units and is about the size of a tissue box, so it can sit at the pharmacy counter where you're already talking about blood pressure. Would trading the wrist monitors for that display work?
CUSTOMER: Actually, yes. Those wrist monitors are dead stock anyway. I'd love to get rid of them. And having it at the counter makes sense. That's where I'm talking to people about their pressure anyway.
REP: What would make you comfortable trying it?
CUSTOMER: I've been burned with front-store products before. I order a case, it doesn't sell, and I'm stuck with it.
REP: That's completely fair. What happened last time, if you don't mind me asking?
CUSTOMER: A sleep-aid brand. Big promotion, nobody bought it, and the rep disappeared. I ate the whole case. It took me a year to sell the last of it at cost, and I think there's still one on the clearance shelf.
REP: That won't happen here. The first order is ninety-day sale-or-return, so anything that hasn't sold by then comes back for full credit, and I'll check in with you at thirty and sixty days. We also include a Know Your Numbers kit, the signage and log sheets for a free blood pressure check day, which tends to move the first case. Does that take the risk off the table for you?
CUSTOMER: It does. Sale-or-return I can work with.
REP: Great. Who else would weigh in on the order?
CUSTOMER: My brother runs the second store. He'll go along if I tell him it works here first. He's more cautious than I am, so if I can show him real numbers after a month, he'll order for his store too.
REP: Then let's start here. I'll put in a one-case order for this store today on sale-or-return, and I'll come back Tuesday the 6th at ten to set up the display and plan a check day with you for later that month. Does that work?
CUSTOMER: Tuesday the 6th at ten is fine. Come after the delivery.
REP: Will do. I'll send the order confirmation and the return terms by email this afternoon.
CUSTOMER: Thanks, Maya.
